editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech softens the reading that Andy Burnham's Scottish 'offer' only reaches for Edinburgh's powers. Its one concrete item runs the other way: devolving DWP employment support to a model 'shaped by Holyrood', plus a look at handing over innovation, enterprise and employability funding. Those are things Westminster now holds.

The gift comes with a condition, though. Support must follow the 'Easterhouse principle', and the stated goal is to push power out 'from Westminster and Holyrood'. London is trading reserved powers for a say in how Edinburgh runs its own internal affairs.

There is also a structural gap the speech skips. In England the vehicle for devolution is the mayor, who receives transport, skills and innovation money. Scotland has no such tier. Its City Region Deals are funding agreements, not governments. Local government, and its reform, sit with Holyrood. Nothing Burnham wants for 'Scotland's regions' can happen unless the Scottish Government first builds institutions to receive it. That gives John Swinney a veto, and gives London a lever in the money it is offering.

Burnham has a further way to apply pressure. Warning that Scottish towns could be 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up' speaks to voters, and over the First Minister's head. The room was full of apprentices on the old Ravenscraig site.

Burnham's diagnosis is that places like Motherwell and Leigh were wrecked by decisions taken far away. That is sound history. But the remedy he offers doesn't quite match the injury. Steel closed because of national industrial and ownership choices, not because a council lacked an employability budget. The real levers in the speech still sit at the centre:
Local control can tailor how people reach jobs. Whether those jobs exist will still be decided in Whitehall.
The early test is modest. The National Economic Council is meeting the devolved leaders for the first time in his premiership. Watch whether it becomes standing machinery or a single set-piece.
